01.note: A slaughterer failed to show his knife to Rava bar Hinnana for inspection. Rava bar Hinnana ostracized him, removed him from his post and proclaimed his meat tereifa, forbidden. When Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi visited, Rava bar Hinnana asked them to look into the man's case, since small children depended on him. Rav Ashi checked the knife, found it intact and declared the meat fit. Mar Zutra asked whether he should not worry about the elder's honor; Rav Ashi answered that they were acting as the elder's own agents, since he had asked them to examine the matter.
01.why: Rav Huna said a slaughterer who does not show his knife to a scholar is ostracized, and Rava said he is removed and his meat declared tereifa; the Gemara reconciled them by whether the knife turns out intact. Here a knife found intact leads to the meat being permitted.

people.name: Rava bar Hinnana
people.about: The Sage who punished the slaughterer and then asked visitors to review the case.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A visiting Sage who worries about Rava bar Hinnana's honor.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A visiting Sage who examines the knife and permits the meat.

terms.meaning: A formal ban by a rabbinic court that cuts a person off from the community until he mends his ways.
An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.

02.note: When Rabbi Zeira moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he ate meat from an animal whose slaughter Rav and Shmuel, the authorities of Babylonia, were reported to rule invalid. The local scholars asked whether he was not from the place of Rav and Shmuel. He replied that the report came from Yosef bar Hiyya (Rav Yosef), who learns from everyone. Rav Yosef heard and was angry: he learned from Rav Yehuda, who was so careful that he even passed on his doubts about which Sage had said something.
02.why: The Gemara has just set out where Rav and Shmuel agree and disagree with Rabbi Yosei on valid slaughter. Afterwards it asks why Rabbi Zeira did not keep the stricter custom of the place he came from, and Abaye and Rav Ashi explain why.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel and ate meat Babylonian authorities forbade.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Also called Yosef bar Hiyya; the Sage who reported Rav and Shmuel's ruling and was angered by Rabbi Zeira's remark.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Yosef's teacher, careful to report even his doubts about who said what.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: The leading Babylonian authorities whose ruling is in question.

terms.meaning: A firstborn male animal was holy and given to a priest; if it had a blemish it could be slaughtered and eaten, but only after a qualified Sage ruled on the blemish.

03.note: A Roman official put a question to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai: one verse in Genesis says birds came from the water, another says God formed them from the ground. Rabban Yohanan answered that they were created from mud, a mix of both. Seeing his students exchange looks, he asked whether it bothered them that he had pushed off his opponent with a flimsy answer. He then told them that birds were really created from water, and are mentioned with the ground only because they were brought to Adam to be named.
03.why: The Gemara has just quoted a teaching that birds, made from mud, need only one of the two signs cut in slaughter, between land animals and fish. This exchange turns on the same question of what birds were made from.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who answers the official one way and his students another.

people.name: the official
people.about: A Roman government official who asks about two verses that seem to contradict each other.

people.name: Adam
people.about: The first man, to whom God brought the birds to be named.

04.note: Rava would check an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa to make sure it had no nicks, and Rabbi Yona shot a bird in flight with it, cutting its neck as a slaughter. The Gemara raises doubts: perhaps the arrow cut the wrong way, from inside the neck? No, it answers: the feathers at the front of the neck were torn, showing the cut came from the front. And how could the blood be covered with earth below and above, as the law requires? The Gemara answers that he set aside the earth of the whole valley beforehand to serve as the earth beneath.
04.why: The Gemara has just learned from a verse about a drawn arrow that slaughter means drawing the blade across the neck, not pressing or striking. This case shows slaughter done with an actual arrow.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who examined the arrow.

people.name: Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa
people.about: The man who shot and slaughtered the flying bird.

terms.meaning: A commandment that when a wild animal or bird is slaughtered, its blood is covered with earth. The Sages read the verse to require earth both under and over the blood.
The windpipe and gullet, which must be cut for a slaughter to be valid.

05.note: A healthy man said, "Write a bill of divorce for my wife." He then went up to the roof, fell and died. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel ruled that if he fell on purpose, the bill of divorce is valid; if the wind pushed him, it is not.
05.why: The Gemara is looking for the source of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that a person's final actions reveal what he meant at the start; it considers this ruling, then argues it may not prove the point, since here the man's words already showed his intent.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who rules on whether the dead man's divorce order holds.

terms.meaning: In Hebrew a get: the document a husband must give his wife to end a marriage. Here the question is whether others may write and deliver it on his instructions.

06.note: Some Arabs came to Tzikuneya and gave rams to Jewish slaughterers, saying: the blood and the fat are for us, the hide and meat for you. Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana sent the question to Rav Yosef: what is the law in such a case? Rav Yosef sent back that Rav Yehuda had said in Shmuel's name that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
06.why: The mishna records a dispute over a Jew slaughtering for a gentile who means it for idol worship; Rabbi Yosei says only the slaughterer's intent matters, and Shmuel ruled like him. This case puts that ruling into practice.

people.name: Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: The Sage who sent the question about the rams.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who answered, citing Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name.

07.note: An animal was brought to Rabba because it might have been clawed by a predator. Rabba began checking its gullet from the outside. Abaye said to him: wasn't it you, Master, who said the gullet can be checked only from the inside? Rabba turned it over, checked inside, found two drops of blood and ruled it tereifa. The Gemara adds that Rabba had only wanted to sharpen Abaye.
07.why: Rabba had taught that the gullet must be checked from the inside, since its outer lining is red anyway, and the Gemara said this matters when an animal may have been clawed. Here is that very case.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The Sage who checks the animal and rules on it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who reminds him of his own teaching.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The food pipe running from the throat to the stomach. A hole in it makes the animal forbidden.

08.note: A bull belonging to the sons of Rav Ukva was slaughtered with a cut that began at the entrance of the gullet and finished in the gullet itself. Rava declared it tereifa, saying he was applying both Rav's stringency and Shmuel's: with Shmuel, the entrance is not a valid place to slaughter, so the first cut counts as damage; with Rav, damage of any size there makes the animal forbidden. The case reached Rabbi Abba, who said the bull was permitted by both Rav and Shmuel, and told them to go tell Rava to pay the owner the value of the bull.
08.why: Rav and Shmuel disagree on the entrance of the gullet: Rav says any hole there is fatal because it counts as part of the gullet; Shmuel says only a large one is, because it is not. Afterwards the Gemara cites a teaching that taking two schools' stringencies together is foolish.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Also called the son of Rav Yosef bar Hama; he declares the bull forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who rules the bull permitted and says Rava must pay.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: Two Sages whose opposing rulings Rava combines.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The point where the throat opens into the food pipe. Sages disagree whether it counts as part of the gullet.

09.note: Rav Tavut said Rava had in fact followed Rav alone. When Rami bar Yehezkel came, he said: do not listen to the rules my brother Rav Yehuda taught in Rav's name. Rav really said that the Sages set a measure for the part of the gullet where slaughter is valid, which shows the entrance is not a valid place to slaughter, and yet he said a hole of any size there is fatal.
09.why: The Gemara has just called Rava's ruling on the bull difficult, since he seemed to combine two opposite stringencies. Rav Tavut defends him: Rav himself held both positions, so Rava followed one Sage.

people.name: Rav Tavut
people.about: The Sage who defends Rava's ruling.

people.name: Rami bar Yehezkel
people.about: Brother of Rav Yehuda; he corrected the rules Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rami bar Yehezkel's brother, who taught rules in Rav's name.

terms.meaning: The point where the throat opens into the food pipe. Sages disagree whether it counts as part of the gullet.

09.flag: Mostly a statement of who said what in Rav's name; the only event is Rami bar Yehezkel's arrival and remark.

10.note: An animal with a cut windpipe was brought to Rav, who sat checking whether most of the windpipe's thickness was cut. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to him: you taught us, our teacher, that it is measured by most of the inner space. Rav sent it to Rabba bar bar Hana, who checked it by the inner space, ruled it kosher, and bought meat from it for thirteen plain istera coins.
10.why: The Gemara has just reported two versions of Rav's view on how much of a windpipe must be cut to make an animal forbidden: most of its thickness, or most of its inner space. Afterwards it asks how Rabba bar bar Hana could permit it after Rav, and eat from it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher who began checking the animal and then sent it on.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who reminds him of his teaching.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Rav's student, who joins in reminding him.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The Sage who rules the animal kosher and buys its meat.

terms.meaning: A small coin.

11.note: A lung with an extra lobe was brought to Mareimar while Rav Aha sat at the door. Rav Aha asked the owner what Mareimar had said, and he answered that it was ruled kosher. Rav Aha told him to go back and bring it before Mareimar again. Mareimar said to him: go tell whoever is sitting at the door that the law does not follow Rava in the case of an extra lobe.
11.why: Rava has just taught that a lung with a missing, extra or misplaced lobe makes the animal tereifa, forbidden. Mareimar's ruling rejects that rule for an extra lobe, and the Gemara then limits where the lobe may be.

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage who ruled the lung kosher.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: A Sage sitting at Mareimar's door who questioned the ruling.

terms.meaning: One of the sections of the lung. Normally an animal has three on one side and two on the other.

12.note: Rabbi Natan told how he once traveled to the cities overseas. A woman came to him whose first son had died after circumcision, and her second as well; she brought her third son to him. He saw the baby was red and told her: my daughter, wait until his blood is absorbed. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
12.why: The Gemara rules that a red or green lung does not make an animal forbidden, and cites Rabbi Natan's babies who recovered from those colors as the proof that such a condition can heal.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: The Sage who advised the mother to wait before circumcising.

people.name: the woman
people.about: A mother who had lost two sons after circumcision.

13.note: Rabbi Natan told how he went another time to Cappadocia. A woman came whose first and second sons had died after circumcision, and she brought her third. He saw the baby was green and had no blood for circumcision in him. He told her: my daughter, wait until his blood comes into him. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
13.why: The Gemara rules that a green lung does not make an animal forbidden, and cites this baby who recovered from a green color as proof that such a condition can heal.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: The Sage who advised the mother to wait before circumcising.

people.name: the woman
people.about: A mother in Cappadocia who had lost two sons after circumcision.

14.note: Rabbi Hananya fell sick, and Rabbi Natan and all the great scholars of the generation came to visit him. They brought before him a lung that could be poured out like water from a jug, and he ruled the animal kosher.
14.why: Rabbi Yohanan had ruled that a liquefied lung is kosher, because damage inside an organ does not count; Rabbi Abba challenged this from the mishna. This case supports the ruling, and Rava then limits it to where the bronchi remain.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The sick Sage who rules the lung kosher.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: One of the scholars who came to visit him.

15.note: Worms were found in an animal's liver. The people of Asia went up to the Sanhedrin in Yavne about it on three festivals, and on the third they permitted it to them.
15.why: The Gemara is listing defects that do not make an animal forbidden, after a liquefied or wasted lung; this case shows that a worm-infested liver is also allowed.

terms.meaning: The high court of the Sages. After the Temple's destruction it sat in Yavne.
The three pilgrimage festivals, when people traveled to the center of Jewish life; here, three trips to put the question.

16.note: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Yosef was walking behind Rabbi Yirmeya in the butchers' market and saw lungs covered in cysts. Hoping to get a ruling, he asked whether the Master wanted some meat. Rabbi Yirmeya said he had no money; Rabbi Yitzhak offered to buy on credit. Rabbi Yirmeya then said: when people came to Rabbi Yohanan with such lungs, he sent them to Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon, who permitted them in his father's name, but Rabbi Yohanan himself did not hold so. Rava adds that when they walked behind Rav Nahman in the market and he saw lungs covered in large cysts, he said nothing to the butchers.
16.why: Shmuel has just ruled that a lung with cysts is kosher. These scenes show what Sages actually did in the market when they saw such lungs.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who tries to draw a ruling out of Rabbi Yirmeya.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The Sage who avoids ruling, then explains Rabbi Yohanan's practice.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who sent such questions to another and did not himself permit.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who permitted such lungs in the name of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who saw such lungs in the market and said nothing.

terms.meaning: Swellings on the lung filled with fluid or pus. The question is whether they mean the animal is forbidden.

16.flag: Combines two separate anecdotes: Rabbi Yirmeya in the butchers' market, and Rava's report about Rav Nahman.

17.note: A needle was found in a cut piece of lung and brought to Rabbi Ami, who thought to rule it kosher. Rabbi Yirmeya (some say Rabbi Zerika) objected from the mishna: a lung that is missing something is fatal, which must mean a loss inside the lung counts. They sent it to Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who also thought to permit it, and the same objection was raised. They sent it back to Rabbi Ami, who ruled it tereifa. Asked why, when the Rabbis permit such a case, he said: they knew their reason, having seen the whole lung; we see only a piece, and perhaps the whole lung would have shown a hole.
17.why: The Gemara has just reported a dispute over a needle found in a lung, and explained it as a question of whether the needle came in by the airway or pierced through. This case shows why Rabbi Ami would not permit when only part of the lung was there.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who first leaned toward permitting, then forbade.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The Sage who raised the objection; some say it was Rabbi Zerika.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Named by some as the one who raised the objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: A second Sage to whom the lung was sent, who also leaned toward permitting.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The early collection of rabbinic law that the Gemara discusses and explains.

18.note: A needle was found in the large duct of an animal's liver. Huna Mar son of Rav Idi ruled it tereifa; Rav Adda bar Minyumi ruled it kosher. They came and asked Ravina, who said: take the robe of those who ruled it tereifa, that is, make them pay the owner for the meat he wrongly threw away.
18.why: The Gemara has just discussed needles found inside organs, and why some can be assumed to have entered without piercing. Ravina's ruling treats a needle in the liver duct the same way.

people.name: Huna Mar son of Rav Idi
people.about: The Sage who ruled the animal forbidden.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Minyumi
people.about: The Sage who ruled it kosher.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who decided that those who forbade it must pay.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.

19.note: Rabbi Hanina's attendant was standing before him, and Rabbi Hanina told him to take off a handful of the fat and give him the rest to eat. Seeing the attendant hesitate, Rabbi Hanina said: you are a Babylonian. Cut it all off and throw it away.
19.why: The Gemara has explained that Sages of the Land of Israel permitted part of a certain fat on the stomach once a handful was removed, while Babylonians forbade all of it; this scene shows the two customs side by side.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who eats the fat once a handful is removed.

people.name: the attendant
people.about: Rabbi Hanina's servant, a Babylonian who hesitates to handle the fat.

terms.meaning: Removing a handful of the upper fat, which counts as the forbidden fat; by the custom of the Land of Israel, the rest could then be eaten.

20.note: Some perforated intestines were brought before Rava. He made fresh holes to compare with the old ones, but they did not look alike. His son Rav Mesharshiyya came, rubbed the new holes, and then they looked alike. Rava asked him how he knew to do that. He answered: how many hands handled these before they came to you, Master? Rava said: my son is as wise in matters of tereifot as Rabbi Yohanan.
20.why: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya has just taught that one may compare holes in the intestines, making a new hole to see whether an old one happened after slaughter. This case shows how to do the comparison fairly.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage before whom the intestines were brought.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: Rava's son, who rubbed the new holes to make the comparison fair.

terms.meaning: Plural of tereifa: animals with fatal defects whose meat may not be eaten, and the laws about them.
Making a new cut next to an old hole: if they look alike, the old hole happened after slaughter and the animal is kosher.
